title: Netflix and Sega Set ‘Crazy Taxi’ Game-to-Film Adaptation
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 14, 2026 8:45am 'Sonic' Courtesy of Fortyseven Communications Netflix is expanding its video game adaptation slate with Sega . The streaming giant is at work on a feature film treatment for Crazy Taxi t o be written by Dan Gregor and Doug Mand, the duo behind the 2025 reboot of The Naked Gun. Neal H. Moritz and Toby Ascher of Original Film and Toru Nakahara, head producer at Sega, are producing the adaptation of the Crazy Taxi game that since a 1999 arcade launch has put players behind the wheel of a fearless cabbie racing the clock through chaotic city streets. Netflix and Sega are also adapting the Sonic game as a new animated series in development with Carlos Stevens and Nakahara, and the Stranger Than Heaven game from RGG Studio and set in early 20th-century Japan to become a live action film, with Nakahara again producing for the video game maker. The Sonic action game franchise began in the 1990s and has sustained strong sales. Related Stories Business Netflix, YouTube and Amazon Launch a Streaming Public Policy Group Movies Netflix to Stream Lee Chang-dong's Films Globally as 'Possible Love' Awards Campaign Heats Up The new multi-title collaboration will look to live-action comedy, kids’ animation and live-action crime adaptations to reflect the range of Sega’s library and expand Netflix’s track record in turning game worlds into scripted and unscripted, live-action and animated films and series. “Great games already have what every adaptation is chasing — characters people love, worlds they know by heart, and fandoms that show up. With Crazy Taxi, Sonic, and Stranger Than Heaven , we get to work across three completely different eras of Sega’s catalog, celebrating everything fans love, while introducing them to new audiences,” Brandon Riegg, vp of nonfiction and transmedia at Netflix, said in a statement. For Sega, the aim is bringing the fan base for its popular games to a new streaming platform, with an eye to franchises. “We’ve watched Netflix take on stories across every kind of format and treat each one with real craft, and seeing that same dedication applied to Sonic, Crazy Taxi and Stranger Than Heaven is something we at Sega are incredibly proud to be a part of,” Shuji Utsumi, president and COO of Sega, said in another statement. Netflix’s earlier video game adaptations include a live action series based on Assassin’s Creed, a live action movie based on the Gears of War game and animated series adaptations for Minecraft, Magic: The Gathering and the Clash of Clans games. title: ‘Crazy Taxi’ Comedy Movie Coming From Netflix and Sega, New ‘Sonic’ TV Series and ‘Stranger Than Heaven’ Film in the Works
full_text: Sep 14, 2026 8:45am PT ‘Crazy Taxi’ Comedy Movie Coming From Netflix and Sega, New ‘Sonic’ TV Series and ‘Stranger Than Heaven’ Film in the Works By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Trump Says He’s the Only AI ‘Guardrail’ Needed and Mocks Anthropic CEO’s Call for AI Slowdown: ‘Pretending to Be a Perfect Little Angel’ 27 minutes ago FCC Chairman Slams James Talarico as Running a ‘Hoax’ With Jimmy Kimmel Interview, Which ABC Punted to YouTube, to Get ‘Clicks and Donations’ 1 day ago Gary Oldman Predicts HBO’s ‘Harry Potter’ Series Will Be ‘More Satisfying’ for Fans Than the Movies 3 days ago See All Courtesy of Sega Netflix has hit the start button on multiple adaptations of Sega hit gaming franchises. The first project under the companies’ new multititle deal is a feature-film adaptation of “ Crazy Taxi ,” Sega’s long-running racing game. The movie will be written by Dan Gregor and Doug Mand — the writing duo behind the 2025 reboot of “The Naked Gun” — with Original Film’s Neal H. Moritz and Toby Ascher and Sega’s Toru Nakahara, the producers behind the Sonic franchises, on board to produce. Related Stories FCC Asks Court to Throw Out ABC's Lawsuit Alleging TV License Review Violates First Amendment, as Agency Repeats Claim the Action Is Unrelated to Jimmy Kimmel or 'The View' Jimmy Kimmel in Talks to Renew Late-Night Show at ABC Netflix and Sega also announced two other adaptations in development: a new animated “ Sonic the Hedgehog ” kids’ series and a movie based on action-adventure game “Stranger Than Heaven.” Popular on Variety “Great games already have what every adaptation is chasing — characters people love, worlds they know by heart, and fandoms that show up,” said Brandon Riegg, VP of nonfiction and transmedia at Netflix, in a statement. “With ‘Crazy Taxi,’ ‘Sonic’ and ‘Stranger Than Heaven,’ we get to work across three completely different eras of Sega’s catalog, celebrating everything fans love, while introducing them to new audiences.” Toru Nakahara, head producer at Sega, commented: “Expect something cute yet cool for ‘Sonic,’ hilariously crazy for ‘Crazy Taxi’ and a badass action drama for ‘Stranger Than Heaven,’ because we’ve got some amazing creative ideas lined up and we are just getting started. The whole team is absolutely thrilled!” In “Crazy Taxi,” which made its arcade debut in 1999, players sit in the driver’s seat as a “fearless cabbie racing the clock through chaotic city streets — flying off ramps, dodging traffic and chasing tips with punk-rock energy that became the series’ signature,” per Sega. The latest title in the franchise, “Crazy Taxi: World Tour,” is scheduled for release in 2027. “We couldn’t be more excited to continue our longstanding relationship with Sega and bring ‘Crazy Taxi’ to life with our partners at Netflix,” Original Film’s Moritz and Ascher said in a statement. “This film is for anyone who’s spent hours behind the wheel of a yellow cab on their Dreamcast, with the music cranked up, smashing through everything in sight just to make the next fare.” Meanwhile, a new animated “Sonic” series is currently in development with Carlos Stevens and Toru Nakahara. The show will present Sonic and his friends as heroes for an upper pre-school audience, touted as a “high-voltage, comedic, yet emotionally grounded series built for kids who want to feel a little edge, a little attitude, and a lot of ‘that’s my crew’ wish fulfillment,” per Sega. Three seasons of Netflix’s “Sonic Prime” 3D animated series are currently available to stream only on Netflix. “Stranger Than Heaven” hails from RGG Studio, developer of the bestselling “Like a Dragon: Yakuza” series, with over 30 million copies sold. The game, set to be released in January 2027, is set in early 20th century Japan, following a foreigner who claws his way from destitute stranger to feared yakuza to entertainment tycoon. Toru Nakahara is set as producer on the film. “We’ve watched Netflix take on stories across every kind of format and treat each one with real craft, and seeing that same dedication applied to ‘Sonic,’ ‘Crazy Taxi’ and ‘Stranger Than Heaven’ is something we at Sega are incredibly proud to be a part of,” said Shuji Utsumi, president and COO of Sega. “The fandoms of these games deserve storytelling that honors what makes each title special, and we know Netflix shares that commitment. This is just the start of what these titles can become.” The new Sega titles will join Netflix’s growing slate of video game adaptations. A note from the SkyShowtime board to CEO Monty Sarhan informed him that it has kicked off a strategic review, “which includes the possibility of a wind-down.” “No decisions have been made, and all options remain under consideration,” added the note, which Deadline has obtained. SkyShowtime was launched as a JV streaming service four years back between Paramount and Comcast as a way of entering European territories that didn’t have access to their own streamers Paramount+ or Peacock. title: Macklemore Dropped From Ed Sheeran Tour After Pro-Palestine Comments During Performances
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All September 14, 2026 8:34am Macklemore performing May 2024 in Melbourne, Australia. Morgan Hancock/Getty Images Macklemore has been dropped from Ed Sheeran ‘s Loop Tour as the rapper drew major headlines for his pro-Palestine speeches during his opening performances on the trek, with Sheeran’s promoter stating Monday that venues set to host the tour threatened to pull out if Macklemore was on the bill. “As the concert promoter for Ed Sheeran’s U.S. Loop Tour, we have been notified by venues on the upcoming U.S. tour dates that they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans,” Messina Touring Group, Sheeran’s longtime concert promoter, said in a statement provided to The Hollywood Reporter . “After discussions with stakeholders, Macklemore will not be performing on the remaining support dates.” Related Stories Music Pink Issues Statement Following Backlash for Critiquing Macklemore's Pro-Palestine Comments: "Standing Up for My Own People" Music Macklemore Responds to Backlash Over "Free Palestine" Plea: "Wanting All Humans to Be Treated Equal Should Never Be Controversial" Reps for Sheeran and Macklemore didn’t immediately respond to request for comment. The news was first reported by Rolling Stone. The move comes over a week after Macklemore, who’s long supported the Free Palestine cause, garnered significant backlash from pro-Israel groups after giving pro-Palestine speeches during performances at MetLife Stadium on Sept. 4 and 5. “A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine,” he told the crowd during his first performance. “I said, ‘Free Palestine!’ I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them.” The Israeli-American Council launched a petition calling to remove him from the tour. The rapper doubled down, telling addressing Jewish members of the crowd during his next show to clarify that “criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace; love for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect, and equality.” He also shared a post on social media last Monday writing that “wanting all humans to be treated equal should never be controversial.” In its statement, Messina Touring Group didn’t specify which venues objected to Macklemore’s spot on the bill, or if it was all of them. He was slated to perform at all of Sheeran’s upcoming North American stadium dates except for the Miami shows on Oct. 29 and 30. Per Rolling Stone, the venues that objected included Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field, Foxbourough’s Gillette Stadium, Atlanta’s Mercedes-Benz Stadium, Indianapolis’s Lucas Oil Stadium, Charlotte’s Bank of America Stadium, Arlington’s AT&T Stadium and Tampa’s Raymond James Stadium. Messina’s statement didn’t specify why the venues pushed back on Macklemore’s performance, though as Rolling Stone noted, a removal from the publicly owned and operated venues (which include all but Gillette Stadium and Bank of America Stadium) due to his previous statements could raise issues a of first amendment rights. Aside from the groups, others who’d voiced out against Macklemore’s actions included Pink, who reposted a call to remove Macklemore from the tour, drawing significant backlash of her own. Days later, she posted a lengthy statement clarifying her views, stating that she was “standing up for my own people, and I thought I knew going in how lonely that would be. And it’s lonelier than that.” THR

title: Pluto Film Boards ‘Ida’ Star Agata Trzebuchowska’s Horror Feature ‘Sick’ Ahead Of Fantastic Fest Premiere + First Teaser
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Well Go USA Entertainment Acquires ‘The Optimist’ For Digital Release On November 17 Canada’s Precious Metal Productions & Black Fawn Distribution Strike Genre Slate Deal – TIFF Beta Cinema Posts Fresh Deals For Trudie Styler’s ‘Up Against It’ Ahead Of TIFF Debut View All September 14, 2026 8:09am Sick Maciej Edelman EXCLUSIVE: Pluto Film has boarded sales for Agata Trzebuchowska’s horror feature Sick ahead of its world premiere at Fantastic Fest in Austin in September, which will be followed by its European debut at the Sitges Film Festival . The unsettling film about the horrors of growing up is the feature directorial debut of Polish director, screenwriter and actress Agata Trzebuchowska, who is best known internationally for her lead performance in Paweł Pawlikowski’s 2015 Oscar winner Ida . Patryk Sielecki and Adrianna Rędzia at Warsaw-based Lumisenta lead produce, while the cast features stars Konrad Kąkol, Katarzyna Łubik, Monika Niemczyk, Julian Świeżewski, and Eliza Rycembel. Related Stories News Firebook Entertainment Signals Move Into Production As First Movie 'Every Heavy Thing' Heads To Sitges News 'Disforia' Trailer: Spanish Horror-Thriller World Premieres At Austin's Fantastic Fest Set against the backdrop of the summer holidays, Sick revolves around sixteen-year-old Maks (Kąkol) and his older sister Emma (Łubik) who are sent to the Polish countryside to care for their ailing grandmother. Watch on Deadline Trapped together in the heavy, stifling isolation of the summer heat, the siblings’ bond begins to shift into something unsettling and difficult to define. As tensions rise and boundaries begin to blur, their grandmother’s frail presence takes on an increasingly disturbing quality, turning a once-idyllic summer into a haunting passage into adulthood. “We are very happy that Sick has found its home at Pluto Film. From our first conversations, we felt that they understood both the film’s provocative nature and the tenderness hidden beneath its genre elements,” said Lumisenta’s Patryk Sielecki. “The world premiere at Fantastic Fest and the European premiere at Sitges are an exciting beginning for the film, bringing it to audiences open to bold and unconventional stories. At the same time, we believe Sick can resonate beyond the genre circuit, as it is ultimately a deeply emotional story about adolescence, desire and dependence, centered on a relationship that crosses every possible boundary.” Pluto Film MD Daniela Cölle praised Trzebuchowska’s bold reinvention of the classic coming-of-age summer tale. “Agata Trzebuchowska has created an atmospheric and unsettling horror film that transforms the oppressive calmness of a summer into a powerful psychological landscape. Rather than coming-of-age story, Sick is the horror of growing up, exploring the fear, confusion, and loss of certainty that accompany the passage into adulthood.” Trzebuchowska shot to fame for her performance in Ida , as a young woman on the verge of taking her vows as a nun, after being scouted in a café by director Małgorzata Szumowska who knew her friend Pawlikowski was struggling to find the right person for the role. Trzebuchowska has eschewed mainstream fame since to forge her own path as a screenwriter and director. Sick follows short films including the Sundance-selected Heat and Vacancy , which also travelled the festival circuit stopping off at Go Short and Flickers’ Rhode Island International Film Festival. She also continues to act and was recently seen in Pete Ohs’ Erupcja alongside Charli XCX, Lena Góra and Will Madden. Sick will premiere in the New Wave sidebar of the Fantastic Fest running from September 17 to 24, 2026. title: Gerbil: Inside Hollywood’s Most Unkillable Rumor
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close Richard Gere’s early image in films like 1980’s American Gigolo, and his reluctance to be interviewed about anything personal, left people wondering about his sexuality. Courtesy Everett Collection When the White House was looking for a way to attack Richard Gere this summer, they went low. Very low — even for this administration. Gere, the politically active 77-year-old actor and philanthropist, had criticized President Trump’s “ignorance” for cuts to the U.S. Agency for International Development. At an event promoting an educational partnership on migration, Gere remarked, “He has idiots around him.” Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, fired back in a July 21 post on X, “Not going to listen to a guy who may have put a gerbil up his ass.” Related Stories Opinion Maybe Paramount-Warner SHOULD Leave L.A. Lifestyle Could the Galliano Met Gala Fiasco Mark the End of Anna Wintour's Reign? And there it was. Again! That those in Trump’s orbit would traffic in the tawdry is hardly news. But the choice of this particular angle of attack reveals the almost supernatural staying power of a rumor, or urban legend, that started roughly four decades ago. I was not surprised to see the White House post. Nothing about the gerbil rumor, not its longevity nor its continued impact, surprises me. You see, I have been investigating everything about it for six years. The Hollywood Reporter is releasing the first two episodes of my podcast series, Gerbil , on Sept. 17, and installments will be released weekly on Thursdays after that. The gerbil legend may be the most essential rumor in Hollywood history because it perfectly reveals how the products of the entertainment industry, deliberately and, more importantly, accidentally, express fears, yearnings, nightmares and dreams that worm themselves eternally into our brains. Or, as Stanford communications professor Fred Turner told me, “This is Richard Gere, an American icon. And so in some sense, the gerbil is not just up Richard Gere’s ass, it’s up America’s ass.” Comedian Sam Kinison, among the first to refer to the story in his act. John Atashian/Getty Images The basic version of the rumor — and it is a rumor, not something for which proof has been publicly produced — is that sometime in the 1980s, Richard Gere showed up at the emergency room of Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles with a gerbil lodged in his rectum that he had inserted for sexual pleasure. Somehow this unsubstantiated story became internationally known with almost no major media explicitly reporting it, and before the modern version of the internet. Barely a decade after the word “meme” was coined to refer to things or ideas that can be imitated and culturally transmitted, and before the concept of memes going “viral” had become known outside academia, the gerbil rumor caught on and caught fire. The first stand-up comedian to ever mention Gere and a gerbil in his act appears to be the late Sam Kinison, who was already noticing how widely it had spread in May 1990. At a Las Vegas show, Kinison’s bit went, “I hope it’s a rumor. I was in Miami last night, the fucking crowd there went nuts. Everybody in the country knows supposedly because … I don’t want to get in trouble, but supposedly — supposedly — I guess he was in the hospital. … How good could this fucking feel?” Calling it a rumor is a kind of shorthand because the gerbil thing is far more than simple gossip about, say, who is dating whom. Jan Harold Brunvand, author of numerous books cataloging urban legends, considered the gerbil rumor “modern folklore.” Brunvand noted that Nobel Prize novelist Gabriel García Márquez was fascinated with trying to discover the origins of what he called “lost stories,” often untraceable tales that keep evolving new details such as one about the man who supposedly discovered a large diamond in the stomach of a fish he caught. Or was it a person who found a gold ring in their order of fried chicken? Or a Bible story about a fish with a coin in its mouth? When exactly the gerbil story started is one of the mysteries I aimed to solve. It also has many variants — although none in the Old Testament. (But maybe in Freud!) Some versions mention the use of a cardboard paper towel roll to guide the gerbil inside. Others insist duct tape or condoms were tools. Still others say the ER visit happened at St. Vincent’s in New York or Hollywood Presbyterian. The gerbil is freed and runs around the ER. The gerbil dies and somewhere are X-rays showing it. It’s not Gere, it’s some other celebrity. A reply from the NSA to the author’s Freedom of Information Act request seeking information on the gerbil hearsay. Courtesy To save you a trip, your AI machine will tell you the Gere gerbil rumor isn’t true. But this is part of what drew me to the story. The machines only know what they can search: digitized magazine articles, Reddit threads and fact-checking sites. I decided to figure out what, if anything, might be true about it and why this particular rumor never seems to die. As an investigator, it was my duty to explore the possibility that he did what people said he did. But even if Gere did not do the deed, what might be learned from the undeniable existence of the urban legend? I used old-school journalism. I interviewed doctors, film directors, actors, talent agents, nurses, would-be witnesses, reporters and many others who were there when the story started. I traced everything that had been written, much of it nondigital, dating back to the story’s murky origins. I studied emergency room records, police reports, criminal case files and filed Freedom of Information Act requests. No one had done this thorough a job to trace the legend’s origins and find out what is true and what is demonstrably false about it — and, more importantly, why the damn thing has outlasted nearly every other gossip item in the history of Hollywood. It has been said that we are living in a “post-truth era,” where people decide what is real based not on facts but on how they feel about an idea. Into this factual breach rush memes that reflect ideas of how the world works, ideas that exhibit what Stephen Colbert called “truthiness” rather than truth. As I was starting the project, I would say the word “gerbil” to anyone I met and record their reactions. One person free-associated revealingly that the idea that celebrities are engaged in weird sexual stuff just feels true. “There’s a sinister underbelly to what really goes on in Hollywood,” they said. Not only does the weirdness make sense to outsiders who assume celebrities are not just like us, the details are so odd, it seems no one could ever make this stuff up, so it must be true. “Conspiracy theories are renowned for making a kind of sense that appeals far more than the truth,” says Susan Blackmore, author of the influential 1999 book The Meme Machine. You don’t have to be over 40 to know the rumor is still everywhere. When the gossip merchant known as Deuxmoi appeared on the Taste of Taylor podcast in November 2024, host Taylor Strecker gushed, “Like the first-ever celebrity conspiracy theory is that [Gere] used to shave gerbils, inject them with cocaine, put Vaseline on them and stick them up his butt. And use them as little vibrators …” The anonymous representative of Deuxmoi replied, “I’ve had people message me and be like, ‘My mom’s friend is a nurse, and he really did come in’ … I think people started to believe it for real. … I don’t believe it, but if I have enough glasses of wine, I might, like, start to believe it.” Young, old or whatever, you could also have heard recent tell of the gerbil legend in one form or another on the podcasts of Joe Rogan, Tig Notaro and Mae Martin, Dax Shepard, and Conan O’Brien; on Family Guy , South Park , Curb Your Enthusiasm and Family Feud ; on TikTok posts that garner hundreds of thousands of views, on Lady Bunny’s Instagram feed, and on Tom Green’s recent stand-up special. I could go on. Lemmiwinks the Gerbil, a character inspired by the Gere rumor, on South Park. Courtesy Why has it lasted? When exactly did it start? Why did it start? Perhaps most importantly as a service both to a country weary of lies and to the widely beloved Richard Gere, is there any chance it’s true, and if it’s not true, is there any way to stop it? I took on this project not to dredge something prurient up, but because it actually struck me as important. Mike Rothschild, who has written books about QAnon and antisemitic conspiracy theories, says that he is sometimes criticized for platforming these things. But he believes that the only way to fight them is by reporting whatever truth can be found. If you believe that truth matters, and that a journalist’s job is to fight lies wherever they arise, you have to ask questions of these theories, rather than being baited into easy criticisms that don’t work to stop conspiracy theories. “So much of it is just the weirdness and the salaciousness and the pointing and laughing,” Rothschild says, “rather than really trying to develop a deeper understanding of the psychological forces behind these movements. Because psychological forces don’t get clicks. Pointing and laughing at weirdos waiting for JFK Jr. to come back gets clicks.” Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles, the setting of most renditions of the tenacious gerbil rumor. Myung J. Chun/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images This is the essence of the gerbil investigation. What psychological forces gave rise to all this in its moment and why does the gerbil persist? To paraphrase the great poem: What rough beast, its hour come round, slouched toward Cedars-Sinai to be born? There is little doubt that the gerbil rumor was a form of homophobia. Gere’s early image in films like American Gigolo and plays like Bent , and his reluctance to be interviewed about anything personal, left people wondering about his sexuality. And the death of Rock Hudson from AIDS in 1985 left the public skeptical about which stars in Hollywood were telling the truth about their preferences. This is part of how Hollywood helped make the gerbil legend, shaping stars to deliver fantasies but telling lies along the way. (There’s more. I’m not spoiling the whole series for the sake of this little article!) In a time now when memes like the Coldplay couple or some celebrity’s too-thin thighs run across your screen only to be overwhelmed by the next hourly outrage or craze, the gerbil rumor comes from a slower time and thus can be slowly examined, its rise teased apart, its makers and its impacts exposed, its truths revealed. The rumor was never harmless. In a pioneering early 1990s academic study of the rumor, ethnographer Norine Dresser reported on an 11-year-old girl telling her that she heard the Gere rumor on the playground and believed it to be true. Rock Hudson, then 29, and his new bride, Phyllis Gates, 25, in 1955. The death of the actor from AIDS in 1985 left the public skeptical about which stars in Hollywood were telling the truth about their preferences. Bettmann/Getty Images Dresser noted that, “Through the acceptance of this legend as truth, the children are internalizing a stigma that will be difficult to destroy. As they grow older and learn more about homosexuality, it will remain linked with lurid bestial behavior. As a result, when these children go through their own sexual awareness and ambivalence, these ideas will remain forever connected, and their own self-images and development may conceivably be damaged.” The 11-year-old in 1993 is 44 now. There is no way Gere could have had any idea the rumor would go as far and last as long as it has. As the years have gone on and his hair has whitened, Gere has become nearly as famous for his charity and his spirituality as his acting. As I’ve dug deeper, I’ve come to believe he might be convinced to see that the gerbil rumor, which has bedeviled him for so long — and my reporting shows it has bothered him — could become a tool for enlightenment. Too grand? After six years on this story, I can tell you the gerbil legend has become my teacher, and I think it can help all of us. My initial request to speak to Gere was denied. “Due to his schedule at this time, Mr. Gere will be unable to participate,” emailed a representative for Gere. The most cogent comments he ever made about the rumor were in a 1991 television interview with Barbara Walters. She asked, “Do you have any idea why anyone would want to hurt you, or embarrass you, or try to smear you?” After some back-and-forth, Gere said, “Does any of this bother me personally? No. People have their own motivations for doing crazy things, you know, and it has nothing to do with me. You know, if I’m a cow and someone says I’m a zebra, it doesn’t make me a zebra.” I expect that as the episodes roll out and Gere and his people have a chance to hear what I’m up to — an attempt, finally, to bring the full truth to bear on the rumor — I will get a call from them. As Tom Hanks did by coming on the podcast Dead Eyes to unravel an old mystery about him, I expect Gere will see this project as something that is of service. Perhaps if, instead of pretending that it has not hurt him, he speaks movingly about the fact that it has, that this is not a victimless little joke, something else new and true will be brought to the story. You’ll have to listen to find out if that’s how it turns out. This story appeared in the Sept. 9 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

title: Moveria Film Acquires ‘No Money No Honey,’ Documentary Set For Imminent Premiere At Camden International Film Festival
full_text: Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew Midnight Madness! A Caped Canadian Prime Minister Stars In ‘Ladies And Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney’ – Toronto Film Festival ‘NAZA’ Review: Israeli Military Accused Of Depraved Indifference To Palestinian Life, Using AI To Kill In Gaza – Venice Film Festival ‘Black Sunflowers’ First Look: Ukraine’s Youth Live Life On The Edge In Propulsive Doc From EP Sean Penn – Toronto Film Festival View All September 14, 2026 8:00am 'No Money No Honey' Mimbre Films/Moveria Film EXCLUSIVE: Moveria Film has acquired international sales rights to No Money No Honey ahead of the documentary’s world premiere at the Camden International Film Festival in Maine. Moveria describes the film directed by Nicole Costa as “a vibrant story of friendship, migration, joy, and resilience” centering on Máxima Mauricio (she/he), “an Argentine non-binary sex worker in New York.” Daniela Camino of Mimbre Films produces along with Costa. No Money No Honey revisits personal VHS tapes recorded by Mauricio between 1991 and 2004, according to a synopsis. “Interweaving this vibrant archival material with post-pandemic 4K footage, the film opens a fluid portal into Máxima’s memory—confronting a childhood marked by abuse and neglect while longing for her golden days across Buenos Aires, Miami, and New York.” Related Stories Documentary Points North Institute Announces 2026 Artist Programs And Points North Forum Ahead of Camden Film Festival Documentary 22nd Camden Film Festival To Showcase New Work By Documentary's Leading Lights: Gibney, Kopple, Oppenheimer, Chin, Vasarhelyi, Poitras & More Lucas Besnard and Yasmin Porangaba negotiated the sales rights deal on behalf of Moveria Film, with producer Daniela Camino representing Mimbre Films. Watch on Deadline Moveria Films “What really drew us to No Money No Honey was the intimacy of Máxima’s story and the way the film brings us directly into her world,” said Lucas Besnard of Paris-based Moveria Film. “I was struck by the contrast between the VHS footage of her past—with all the energy, glamour, friends, and parties—and her life in New York in 2020. Having lived in New York myself, I connected with this side of the city. Máxima is incredibly endearing, and through her story, you get a sense of a queer community and a reality that deserves to be seen and better understood. That’s what made us want to bring the film into Moveria’s catalogue.” Ceskary Avitia of Moveria Film added, “Coming from Mexico, I know how much prejudice surrounds sex work and trans identity. What drew me to this film is that it doesn’t try to convince you of anything; it just asks you to listen to Máxima’s own voice and to the VHS tapes she filmed of her life. Through her archive, someone’s story opens up into an entire community—her friends, their world, and their shared history of trauma and resilience. Nicole Costa gives voice to a community rarely heard on screen, and everyone deserves the chance to tell their own story.” Mimbre Films In a statement, producer Daniela Camino of Mimbre Films commented, “Working with Moveria has been a turning point for No Money No Honey ’s international debut. Their experience and personalized approach are just what a film like ours needed. We are truly confident we will reach audiences around the globe.” No Money No Honey is programmed in Cinematic Vision Award competition at CIFF, the prestigious all-documentary festival that runs Sept. 17-20 in mid-coast Maine. The acquisition expands Moveria’s slate of “bold, auteur-driven international cinema,” according to a release. Founded in 2025, Moveria is an independent production, international distribution, and cultural mediation company “born from a collaboration between tech developers Arnaud Schoenher and Tristan de Oliveira and arts and culture professionals Ceskary Avitia and Isotta Tassoni… Moveria Film merges custom digital tools—including modeling, automation, and optimization—with traditional film production and distribution frameworks, bringing a novel approach to cinema grounded in dialogue across diverse fields to foster new creative experiences, fresh perspectives, and bold narratives about the world around us.” No Money No Honey , running time 80 minutes, is directed by Nicole Costa and written by Costa, Daniela Camino, and Melisa Miranda. Daniela Camino and Costa produced the film. The cast includes Máxima Mauricio Rodas, Sebastian Quiencke a.k.a. La Baronesa Ditra, Antonia Martinez, Nellie Benittez, Mila Miller, Darius M. title: ‘The Last Photograph’ Review: Zack Snyder Tries Indie Filmmaking on for Size, With Painfully Ponderous Results
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Michael Rechtshaffen Plus Icon Michael Rechtshaffen View All September 14, 2026 7:22am 'The Last Photograph' Toronto Film Festival After an extended sojourn working in the DC Extended Universe, successful filmmaker Zack Snyder casts off those studio shackles and goes full-on indie with The Last Photograph , a highly personal, long-in-gestation, self-styled Western that trades lavish studio sets for the wide-open spaces of Colombian location shoots. But while the change of pace undoubtedly felt liberating, the end result comes across as a leaden misfire. Overstuffed with pretentious symbolism and flatly delivered, vapid dialogue that constantly overstates the obvious, the ultraviolent film — about a rogue government agent who enlists the help of a heroin-addicted shutterbug to take revenge on the murder of his brother and sister-in-law and rescue their abducted kids — is certain to be regarded as a major disappointment by Snyder’s rabid fan base. Related Stories Movies Six Years After Starring Father Died Soon After TIFF Short Premiere, 'Strong Son' Director Returns With Grief Drama Movies 'Seventeen' Director Justin Ducharme Talks Portraying Struggling Sex Workers as BFFs in Gritty Vancouver The Last Photograph The Bottom Line Small canvas, big misfire. Venue: Toronto International Film Festival (Special Events) Cast: Stuart Martin, Fra Fee, Constanza Andrade, Marlon Moreno, Quique Mendoza, Gustavo Angarita, Ed Hughes, Pedro Calvo-Anca, Mia Calvo, Jackie Kay, Jose Restropo Director: Zack Snyder Screenwriter: Kurt Johnstadt 2 hours, 15 minutes Positioned as a premium centerpiece for TIFF’s inaugural market, where it is hoping to secure a distribution deal, the 135-minute slog was given Special Event status, meaning there will be no repeat screenings beyond its world premiere on Sunday evening. Many of those who exited the theater shared the same expression of disbelief over what they had just experienced. We don’t know it when we’re first introduced to him, but Ethan Black (Stuart Martin), who would appear to be a loner sheep herder, is actually an ex-DEA agent who thought he had left his more violent ways behind him. That is until his young niece and nephew are kidnapped at a birthday party following the fatal shooting of his diplomat brother and the latter’s wife (Constanza Andrade). Regarded as something of a God-like presence by the locals, Black turns avenging angel as he teams up with Joe Wallace (Fra Fee), a junkie war photographer — when he’s not shooting conflict, he shooting heroin — who snapped a photo of the children’s mother at the moment she was shot in cold blood. Wallace is instrumental in Black identifying and tracking down her killer and hopefully bringing home those missing kids. And so, the two men with very different life philosophies proceed to journey ever deeper into the South American heart of darkness, with a little bit of The Searchers thrown in for good measure. A whole lot of very intense blood-spilling ensues, but to be honest, it often comes as a welcome distraction from screenwriter Kurt Johnstadt’s monotonous dialogue and clunky expository character motivations that are needlessly underscored by redundant flashbacks. Who would’ve thought, for example, that Wallace was constantly hiding behind the lens of his trusty camera as a way to numb himself to the horrors of the world? And when he tells Black, “I’m not good at being noble,” was that a deliberate nod to the Humphrey Bogart line in Casablanca ? And, if so, why? Saddled with characters that play more like memes than fully inhabited human beings, both Martin and Fee , let’s just say, have made a better impression elsewhere. Mexican actress Andrade, whose character happens to be the love of Black’s life, fares somewhat better, but still isn’t quite let off the hook by the film’s overall tendency to portray its female characters in the same misogynistically objectified light. The xenophobic portrayal of the area’s indigenous population is a whole other, uncomfortable issue. To be fair, Snyder, who’s also credited as the film’s cinematographer, captures no shortage of admittedly stirring images throughout, especially those involving flickering light and brooding shadows. The constant intrusion of yellow butterfly imagery, on the other hand, begins to border on the overindulgent long before one final, eyeball-rolling appearance. In the absence of the filmmaker’s trademark super-sized canvas, the usual techniques can’t help but feel forcefully out of scale here. Still, one might justifiably argue that Snyder at least deserves credit for going out on a limb — even if it can’t help but snap under the weight of all that affectation. Full credits Venue: Toronto International Film Festival (Special Events) Production companies: Stone Quarry, Hollywood Gang Cast: Stuart Martin, Fra Fee, Constanza Andrade, Marlon Moreno, Quique Mendoza, Director: Zack Snyder Screenwriter: Kurt Johnstadt Producers: Zack Snyder, Deborah Snyder, Gianni Nunnari, Wesley Coller Executive producers: Alessandro Salem, Kurt Johnstadt, William Doyle, Juan Pablo Solano, Simon Beltran Director of photography: Zack Snyder Production designer: Diego Garcia Costume designers: Stephanie Porter, Johanna Buendia-Para Music: Hans Zimmer, Omer Benyamin, Steven Doar Editor: Melissa Remenarich-Aperlo Sales: CAA 2 hours, 15 minutes THR

title: SkyShowtime May Be Sold or Shut Down, Board Warns In Memo Shared With Staff (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 14, 2026 7:15am SkyShowtime CEO Monty Sarhan Photo by Pablo Cuadra/Getty Images for SkyShowtime Comcast and Paramount Skydance are launching a “review of strategic options” for their European joint venture streaming service SkyShowtime , The Hollywood Reporter has learned. While no decisions have been made as of yet, shutting down the business is one of the options on the table. The board of the JV informed SkyShowtime CEO Monty Sarhan of the strategic review Monday in a letter, which was viewed by THR . Sarhan subsequently shared it with staff at the company. “SkyShowtime operates in one of the most competitive markets in our industry. Despite the excellent work of the team and the strength of what you and the team have built, the landscape continues to evolve rapidly, and remains highly challenging,” the board’s letter stated. “Against that backdrop, SkyShowtime’s shareholders are commencing a review of strategic options for the business, which includes the possibility of a wind down. No decisions have been made, and all options remain under consideration.” SkyShowtime combines content from NBCUniversal and Sky Studios as well as Paramount, effectively offering a service with the combined programming might of Peacock and Paramount+ in the U.S. The service was first announced five years ago, and serves more than 20 different countries in Europe. In his note, Sarhan noted that SkyShowtime currently has “several million subscribers and stand in scale alongside the most established players in the market.” However, with a rapidly changing media environment (when the JV was formed, David Ellison had not yet acquired Paramount, and he is currently seeking to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery), and with media giants reexamining their streaming strategies, the experiment may well be nearing its end. In his note to SkyShowtime employees, Sarhan wrote that: “I know this news creates uncertainty and, as we work through what comes next, my priority and that of the leadership team, is to be there and support all of you. Together, we have created a community and culture with empathy, opportunity, and innovation at its heart. Whatever comes next, we will all continue to be there for one another.” SkyShowtime’s board, in its letter, noted that the companies are taking their time to figure out what the best path forward will ultimately be. “We know the most important question this raises is what it means for the SkyShowtime team. This update is the beginning of a dialogue, not the end of one,” the board wrote. “The service continues to operate as normal for customers and partners, and every role continues unchanged today. At this time, we ask that the team remain focused on bringing our audiences the quality of service and programming you have all expertly delivered over the years, and maintaining momentum of the operating business into 2027. “Where any proposal could affect employees, we will follow the information and consultation processes required in each of our markets,” it continued. “Final decisions will be made after those conversations have taken place.” THR

title: Ridley Scott Reveals Directing Secrets to Fellow Helmer Jimmy Chin: “Don’t Listen to Anybody”
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Jimmy Chin Plus Icon Jimmy Chin View All September 14, 2026 7:15am Ridley Scott on the set of 'Black Hawk Down.' Columbia/Courtesy Everett Collection In climbing, we have a word for talking up your own accomplishments — spraying . You’re not supposed to do it. The rule makes things awkward for someone promoting a documentary about climbing, which is what I was doing in early 2016. But that’s how I wound up at an awards-circuit luncheon in New York City seated next to Ridley Scott and across from Matt Damon. The whole point of luncheons like that is to convince members of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences to give your film an Oscar. It’s all very uncomfortable. Publicists handle the choreography, making sure you meet the right people and sit next to the right people. I was there for Meru , which had come out the summer before. Ridley and Matt were on the campaign trail for The Martian . I already knew Matt because one of his trainers is a close friend of mine. I’d worked out with Matt while he was training for his film Elysium . I’d never met Ridley Scott. Related Stories Movies 'Everest: The Other Side' Review: A Frustrating, Guiltily Compelling Portrait of the Triumph and Tragedy of Extreme Mountaineering Movies 'Coyote vs. Acme' Snags No. 2 With $15.4M as 'Spider-Man' Nears 'Avatar 2'; 'Dog Stars' Put to Sleep I was intimidated. One of the first movies I’d ever seen was Alien — back in the early eighties, when I was about 10 years old and hanging out at my friend Chris’s house in Mankato. We watched Alien together and it blew my mind. I wasn’t thinking about who was directing the movie, and I certainly didn’t know who Ridley Scott was. All I could think about was the alien exploding out of John Hurt’s chest. Years later, when I was an undergraduate at Carleton, I took a film class and we all joined the professor to go see Blade Runner (The Director’s Cut) at a theater in Minneapolis. When I put two and two together and realized that this guy named Ridley Scott had directed both, he suddenly became an icon in my mind. By the time I found myself next to him at that awards-campaign luncheon, I knew that his body of work was vast and brilliant, packed with other timeless titles like Thelma & Louise, Black Hawk Down, Hannibal, Gladiator, Prometheus, Robin Hood — and thirty other unforgettable features. Ridley Scott was that rarest of beasts in Hollywood, a guy who could make one riveting blockbuster after another while maintaining absolute creative integrity. Nobody else had a body of work that large in which every frame was handmade. Sitting next to him, the question I had was not what he knew. It was how he had stayed in motion at that level for this long. This interview is excerpted from ‘Rules to Live By: How Extraordinary Lives Define What Really Matters’ by Jimmy Chin (out Sept. 29) Celadon Books I barely spoke to Ridley at that luncheon; I was too scared. A few years later, when I started making Nyad , I found myself thinking about Ridley because of the sheer number of decisions that a director has to make every day during production, from which framed picture you want hanging on one wall of one room on one set — How about this picture? Or this one? Or maybe this one? — to which fifty out of a hundred possible extras should appear on the beach and whether one particular extra should wear the red shirt or the blue shorts. On and on: Every single detail goes through the director. The people running every production department — art, camera, lighting, wardrobe, stunts — are constantly coming to you with options inside of options inside of options. Yes or no? What do you think? I wound up loving the sheer intensity of directing Nyad . It also drove my admiration for Ridley to a new level. Nyad is a relatively contained story, set entirely in the present day and with only a handful of characters. Compare that to Blade Runner or Alien or Robin Hood , for which the set designs alone were vastly more complicated than anything I’ve ever contemplated; then add the vast landscapes and thousands of extras for Kingdom of Heaven, Black Hawk Down , and Prometheus . In the decade since that lunch, he’s directed seven more features — Alien: Covenant, All the Money in the World, The Last Duel, House of Gucci, Napoleon, Gladiator II and The Dog Stars. Seven films in ten years, in a stretch of life when most directors have long since stopped working. Years later, while I was working on my new book of interviews with people I admire, I reached out to Ridley. Of all the directors I might have asked to talk to, he was the one I wanted most. To my surprise, he said yes. “My parents were great,” Ridley said. “There was no strange upbringing. Nothing odd happened. By the end of the war, my father was an acting brigadier general dealing with D-Day and then with the Marshall Plan rebuilding Germany. I spent 1947 on a troop ship in my little overcoat with my name on the label in case I got lost, and my own little gas mask, going down the Rhine to be met by my father’s driver. I was there for five years, from 1947 to 1952. My parents would turn me loose every morning and say, ‘Out you go, be back by five. Don’t kill yourself and don’t die.’ My mom was four foot eleven. She said she was five feet. But Dad was away so often that Mom was the man of the house. Tony Scott, my younger brother, was thirteen or fourteen and already rock climbing on granite when he said to me, one day, ‘Hey, you want to go climbing?’ We hit the Yorkshire Dales on bicycles. We went to this granite tower and Tony says, ‘I’ll go up first.’ So Tony nips up the wet granite with a rope. It’s probably eighty feet, it’ll kill you if you fall. And he lobs the rope over the top in the fog, so I can’t see him, and he says, ‘Ready? I’ve got you, up you come.’ I struggled up about fifty feet. Then I said, ‘My arms are giving out!’ He said, ‘You’re using too much arm! You got to use balance.’ I peeled off and swung like a dead spider on a rope. My fourteen-year-old brother saved my life. “My mother taught me to be relentless, too. If you do what we do for a living” — make movies — “you better be relentless. You better not take no for an answer. Deal with life as it comes at you. I’ve just spent months working on a project and then the studio suddenly said, ‘It’s not the right time.’ I said, ‘What?’ So I will now bypass them and take it somewhere else. That’s the job. And very parallel to the importance of being relentless is a cool assessment of what you’re going to do.” *** Ridley went to school in the 1950s at the Royal College of Art in London, where one of his classmates was the young David Hockney. After college, Ridley designed sets for the BBC and directed television commercials. He says he made more than two thousand commercials before he was done, and he credits that commercial work for his later success. Art school taught him what he wanted to say; commercials taught him how to make an audience listen. The film I most wanted to ask Ridley about was Black Hawk Down . I’ve watched it twenty-five times. I should have probably asked about Blade Runner, Alien , or Gladiator , too, but I love Black Hawk Down . I’d always wondered how Ridley shot it, how he made everything feel so visceral. He somehow put you simultaneously inside and outside the action and maintained continuity through it all. The cameras seemed to be everywhere all at once. When I asked him how he came to make it, Ridley said, “My best friend, the person I’ve known the longest in Hollywood, is Jerry Bruckheimer. When Jerry was an advertising-agency producer doing commercials, I’d just finished shooting one with him in San Francisco and we were driving to the airport and he said, ‘I’m going to get out of this business. I’m going to go into the movies.’ I said, ‘Yeah, sure.’ Then he did four movies with my brother, Tony Scott — Top Gun, Beverly Hills Cop II, Days of Thunder and Crimson Tide. Somehow the films Jerry was doing were not for me, I wasn’t interested, but then he came to me with Black Hawk Down and I said, ‘OK, I’ll do this.’ The story covered a simultaneous eighteen-hour action” — the Battle of Mogadishu, involving 160 U.S. soldiers in multiple helicopters and ground vehicles across an entire city — “so it took a lot of sorting out visually.” Ridley told me this came out of something he had learned by shooting all those commercials: how to have multiple cameras shooting at once from different angles without any of those cameras appearing in any other camera’s shot. For Black Hawk Down , Ridley decided that he would, in essence, stage the entire sprawling Battle of Mogadishu, with all its moving parts, as a series of simultaneous actions, and have eleven camera units capturing everything together. “Simultaneous insanity,” he called it. “But it meant that I could crosscut between all these simultaneous events — from when the Black Hawk helicopters come into base, take off again; cut to the High Street, helicopters passing over, scattering chocolates; Night Hawk helicopters coming into base, landing, taking off; guys running into the building. Cut. That’s one take of eleven cameras but it gets every component of the action and lets me cut it all together.” I could not imagine running a production that complex, much less walking into a financing meeting and saying, “Oh, and by the way, for my next movie, I’m going to need eleven cameras and eleven camera crews.” Ridley wasn’t having it. “Shooting with eleven cameras simultaneously makes it cheaper,” he said. “Because it takes fewer than half as many days. That allowed me to shoot Napoleon in 42 days instead of 130. Gladiator II in 47 days instead of 120.” *** When I was out raising money for Nyad , I kept running into the classic concern about anyone making the jump from directing documentaries to directing narrative — I’d never worked with actors before. People knew I could tell a story, that I knew how to frame a shot and move people through it, and that I had my own personal visual language. But still: Will he be able to get the best performance out of the actors? Intuition told me it wouldn’t be so different from working with elite athletes, which I’d done for years. Once we got the financing to make Nyad with Annette Bening and Jodie Foster , I reached out for advice from the handful of actors I knew. They all said the same thing: “The biggest tell of a first-time director is that they won’t stop directing.” An inexperienced director is constantly saying things to the actors like “I want you to feel this, or really bring out that sense of conflict between you and her.” In other words, a first-time director just can’t shut up. One friend after another told me, “If you do that, you will lose your actors, you will likely lose everybody on set too because they will all feel it and you probably won’t make your day.” Director Jimmy Chin, far right, on the set of Nyad in 2023. From left: Karly Rothenberg, director Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi, Annette Bening, Jodie Foster, Diana Nyad, Bonnie Stoll, Rhys Ifans. Kimberley French/Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection Ridley mostly affirmed what I’d heard from friends. “Actors don’t want the history of life between every fucking take. They want ‘faster,’ ‘slower,’ or ‘louder.’ So, ‘Jodie! Faster!’ Because an actor at that level has already thought about what they’re going to do. So my biggest compliment to an actor might be, ‘Wow, where the fuck did that come from?’ And they’ll say, ‘What, you don’t like it?’ And I’ll say, ‘No, I love it! That’s me being blown away! You got it! Want to go again?’ And when they reply, ‘No,’ I say, ‘Exactly.'” Ridley made it clear that, to his way of thinking, this level of trust has to apply to every member of a team — any team, trying to accomplish anything extraordinary. “You can’t do shit by yourself. You need help, and the better I get at my trade, the better the people helping me need to be so that we can all go to the next level together. You cannot do what I do without a handpicked team. Even the final stuff like editing is an art form. It’s the final rewrite. I pick my team little by little. You find out who works well with you, and cameramen who don’t mind if I position the cameras, who won’t get pissed off.” “My unit on Napoleon was twelve hundred personnel. It’s a fucking town. Two hundred horses, five hundred extras. There’s wardrobe, makeup. One morning, I got there and they told me, ‘Joaquin [Phoenix, who played Napoleon] is in the trailer and won’t come out.’ I found him and said, ‘What’s up?’ Joaquin said, ‘Who’s all this for?’ I said, ‘It’s for you dude.’ He went, ‘Oh God,’ and then he passed out. Or take Gladiator II. We built the Roman Colosseum full scale. Paul Mescal comes on and looks around at this gigantic set with hundreds of extras and I get out in front of it. I said, ‘Forget it. It’s only a fucking set.’ I will not let him dwell in terror.” Ridley talks a lot about decisiveness: faster, alone, less consultation with others. “As a director,” he told me, “I always have everything planned, but even now I might show up in the morning with a new thought. Another direction. You have to listen to yourself and then just say, to everyone else, ‘This is where we’re going, no questions.’ Once you’re driving the car and doing 205 miles per hour, you can’t take advice. But watch out, too. Do not lose your temper. I’ve got a real fucking temper, and I learned to rein it in pretty early. Kicking doors and punching walls doesn’t work because people don’t respect it and it makes them nervous, so they won’t perform properly. You have to be calm, ideally humorous, and always determined and sure of yourself and your vision. If you’re sure, they’re not going to question it. I worked with a very good actor recently. He said, ‘How are you so sure?’ I said, ‘I’m not.’ You gotta hide your fear. “There’s only one critic. Yourself. It’s a bit like being a painter. Do not listen to the fucking tutor. You’re on your own with the canvas. You make the assessment, you make the decision. Blade Runner got torn apart by Pauline Kael in The New Yorker . I’d never even met her, and her article was so destructive. But now I have those four pages framed and hung on the wall so I’ll never forget: ‘Don’t listen to anybody, just yourself.'” “The thing that’s taken me the longest to learn is, ‘Make your mind up faster.’ Ridley said that, after the production of Alien , his eldest brother, Frank, got a terminal diagnosis of melanoma. “That damaged me quite heavily. While he was dying, I was working on an adaptation of Dune . I prepped it with the company, and we were going to shoot in Mexico City, and I went to Mexico City and said, ‘I don’t want to spend the next ten months here.’ I went back and stayed with my brother. So I had a big gap before the next movie. It took me too long to decide what to make next.” Five years elapsed before Ridley made his next film, Blade Runner . After that, though, his pace accelerated — and he has now made twenty-nine features. “Just make the movie,” he said. “Don’t overthink it. If you like it, do it. And then, ‘Next.’ And, ‘Next.’ You’re not going to make the meaning of life. I mean, you might eventually, but you’ll only do that when you climb to it.” *** I told Ridley that part of my motivation for working on this book was turning fifty and looking at life’s back half. So he had advice for me there, too. “Early on,” he said, “my idea of success was an E-Type Jaguar, but now I drive a Prius that I’ve had for ten years. People say, ‘What’s the matter, you bankrupt?’ I say, ‘No, I’m trying to save the world.’ Less is more. You can get your Rolls-Royce and your Porsche and your Land Rover, and then you stare at them in your garage and think, ‘Why have I got three cars?’ Once that thought hits you, you get sensible. But if it never hits you, then you carry on being an idiot.” I told Ridley this was a climber’s mentality. Ridley said, “I think of a climb in terms of a beginning, middle, and end. There’s a parallel there with life. You tend not to think about the end. I’m 88 now, and I tend not to ever think about what happens next. I really don’t dwell on it, and I just consider my good fortune about being healthy in full mind and body. That’s an incredible stroke of luck. So I just carry on with that, see how long it’ll take me. At the same time, though, it’s a bit like a climb: The nearer you get to the top is really when you got to watch that you don’t get careless. Alex Honnold visualizes every move on El Cap before he ever leaves the ground. Ridley does the same thing on paper. On a final note, I once asked Ridley what he knows now that he wished he’d known as a younger man. His reply stuck with me: “Nothing. I did OK. Just never forget the steps you took. It’s called experience. Little by little, you’re making decisions intuitively. Everything I do now is intuitive — even controlling my anger on my way into a meeting that’s going to be stupid. I once kicked a wall in a trailer. My foot went through the wall and I fell on the carpet. I lay there, incredibly embarrassed. I’ll never do that again.” From Rules to Live By: How Extraordinary Lives Define What Really Matters by Jimmy Chin Copyright © 2026 by the author and reprinted by permission of Celadon Books. THR

title: Netflix, YouTube and Amazon Launch a Streaming Public Policy Group
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 14, 2026 7:01am The sun sets behind the U.S. Capitol Dome on September 4, 2026 in Washington, DC. Photo by Finn Gomez/Getty Images A new public policy group has been formed in Washington D.C., one that will represent the interests of streaming platforms. The Streaming Access and Choice Alliance (SACA) launched Monday, with Netflix , YouTube and Amazon as its founding members. TechNet, the tech public policy group, is leading the new venture, with Mike Ward, TechNet’s senior VP of federal policy and government relations also leading SACA. “Americans want more content choices and flexibility in how and where they watch their favorite programming, including sports and other live events,” said Ward in a statement. “Streaming and digital entertainment companies offer audiences better features and value for their money. The industry and its customers deserve a dedicated voice in Washington, D.C., advocating for policies that enable innovation and address the needs of today’s consumers.” While Big Tech and Big Hollywood are well-represented in D.C., streaming services are not currently well represented in D.C. The Motion Picture Association looks out on behalf of entertainment companies and studios, while TechNet and other groups work on behalf of tech giants. A previous lobbying group, the Internet Association, shuttered a few years back. SACA meanwhile will “advocate for policies that expand consumer access to high-quality content, preserve choice, and support the innovative viewing experiences consumers value.” Streamers, after years of growth, are facing fresh pressure from the public and from government officials, as prices continue to rise and with programming splintered across so many platforms. Sports have become a particularly big boogeyman, with Prime Video and Netflix each hosting exclusive NFL games this season, and with the FCC and broadcasters lobbying for regulators to require sports to be available for free on broadcast stations. Indeed, the SACA website certainly suggests that the sports push will be a top priority for the group. “Streaming provides audiences and sports fans more choice and more control. SACA makes sure Washington hears them,” the group’s website states. David Ellison, the CEO of Paramount, has argued that his quest to secure Warner Bros. Discovery is being done in part so that his company can compete with the tech giants. THR

Related Stories News Nicolas Cage's Malibu Mansion Damaged by Massive Sinkhole Amid Coastal Erosion Lifestyle Did Jeff Bezos Just Buy a $200 Million Condo in Beverly Hills? These agents powered through the challenges — a few even outperformed 2025 — thanks to social media, innovative partnerships and a love of the game. Josh, Matt and Heather Altman and Jacob Greene Courtesy of Subject (4) The Altman Brothers Team DOUGLAS ELLIMAN Reality stars Josh, Matt and Heather Altman and Jacob Greene had another epic year, with more than $1 billion in deals from July 2025 to July 2026. Among the highlights were the local-record-breaking sale of a $25 million mansion in the coveted Encino neighborhood of Royal Oaks. They also hold the co-listing to the $39.8 million Hollywood Hills mansion built for Full House creator Jeff Franklin. “Good product that is priced correctly is selling,” Josh says. “I think we’ll continue to see buyers move quickly and aggressively for the right properties.” Cindy Ambuehl Courtesy of Subject Cindy Ambuehl CHRISTIE’S INTERNATIONAL REAL ESTATE SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA It was another stellar year for former actor Ambuehl, who totaled $355.9 million in sales year-to-year. Her standout deals included the $25 million sale of David E. Kelley and Michelle Pfeiffer’s Pacific Palisades estate; representing Kevin Nealon (also in the Palisades); and the sale of a Frank Gehry-designed Santa Monica home to Jason Blum. Ambuehl is heartened by the continuing recovery of the Palisades and Malibu. “There is real momentum returning to the Westside,” she says. “You can feel people becoming excited about the future of these communities again.” Santiago Arana Courtesy of Subject Santiago Arana THE AGENCY Known as the ultimate closer, Arana continues to be a major player in the market. In May, he represented Kamala Harris and Doug Emhoff in their purchase of an $8.15 million beach house in Point Dume, Malibu. “I genuinely believe this is one of the best times to be a buyer in Los Angeles,” he says. “The city is due for a strong comeback, and when that happens, these opportunities will be gone.” Rochelle Atlas Maize Courtesy of Subject Rochelle Atlas Maize NOURMAND AND ASSOCIATES Claiming more than $3.5 billion in career sales, Atlas Maize is known for her innovative media campaigns. Big closings this year included the $22.5 million sale of the historic “Roxbury Estate” in Beverly Hills, the onetime home of Casablanca director Michael Curtiz. “A million page views are wonderful,” she says. “One qualified buyer is better.” $4M Hollyridge House — 2356 Hollyridge Drive — listed by Rochelle Atlas Maize of Nourmand & Associates. Courtesy of Nourmand and Assoc. Ernie Carswell Courtesy of Subject Ernie Carswell SOTHEBY’S INTERNATIONAL REALTY After a messy split with Douglas Elliman, Carswell is thrilled that his team has found a new home at Sotheby’s. “I’ve learned the value of a true international company within our industry,” he says. With famous clients including the Chandler family and the late Raquel Welch, he now holds the co-listing for Angelina Jolie’s famed “Cecil B. DeMille Estate” in Los Feliz, on sale for $29.8 million. Jordan Cohen Courtesy of Subject Jordan Cohen REMAX Ranked the No. 1 ReMax agent worldwide, Cohen has long been known for his work with such A-list actors as Sylvester Stallone and more than 150 pro athletes, among them Reggie Miller, Shaquille O’Neal, Pete Sampras and Pau Gasol. He kept up his streak in 2026, scoring a big win with a major NBA star. “Selling Anthony Davis’ home in Bel-Air for $32 million was my most noteworthy sale for 2026 so far,” he says. Chris Cortazzo Courtesy of Subject Chris Cortazzo COMPASS With $815 million in sales from July 2025 to July 2026, Malibu ace Cortazzo has been at the front lines of the area’s post-fire recovery. He now holds the listing to the storied $90 million Point Dume Mediterranean mansion featured on The O.C. “Fortunately, we don’t have the ULA [mansion] tax in Malibu,” he says. “That has been a real advantage for our market, particularly at the luxury level.” Drew Fenton Courtesy of Subject Drew Fenton CAROLWOOD ESTATES With $9 billion in career sales, Fenton has attracted a starry clientele that includes Anthony Russo, James Packer, Eva Chow, Nick Candy and the estate of Bob Newhart. In May, he held the list on “The Peak,” a residential lot in Beverly Hills that sold for $31.8 million. Sally Forster Jones Courtesy of Subject Sally Forster Jones COMPASS Forster Jones counts among her clients Candy Spelling, Barbra Streisand and Chrissy Teigen and John Legend. Notable sales include a new Ramtin Ray Nosrati-designed Brentwood home for $24.38 million. In November, she became the recipient of the inaugural Compass Lifetime Achievement Award, given by Compass SoCal, for her years of success and contribution to the Los Angeles real estate industry. $100M La Fin, at 1200 Bel Air Road, listed by Sally Forster Jones of Compass. Courtesy of Compass Tomer Fridman Courtesy of Subject Tomer Fridman BEVERLY HILLS ESTATES Known as “Hollywood’s agent of record,” Fridman is the Kardashian-Jenner family’s go-to broker. He recently held the co-listing for Lori Loughlin and Mossimo Giannulli’s Hidden Hills estate that sold for $12.6 million. His portfolio reads like a map of trophy properties in Los Angeles, including 620 Arkell Drive in Beverly Hills, sold at $100 million, and Bel-Air’s La Fin, which brought $99.95 million. “The most sophisticated buyers don’t necessarily want the biggest house,” says Fridman, who recently left Christie’s for Beverly Hills Estates. “They want the house that is a home in every sense of the word.” Carl Gambino Courtesy of Subject Carl Gambino COMPASS As the Gambino Group continues its global expansion, it is hardly abandoning its L.A. base of operations. Major sales include the former Beverly Hills estate of Michael Caine and, later, Ricky Martin, which closed in December for $35 million. He also repped the buyer of Bruce Willis’ former $41.25 million Benedict Canyon estate. “Professionally, this has been my most successful year yet,” he says, “but what I’m most proud of is the team we’ve built.” Ginger Glass Courtesy of Subject Ginger Glass COMPASS With clients including Kylie Jenner, Mark Wahlberg, Jennifer Lopez, Cameron Diaz and Benji Madden, the THR list mainstay continues to find new ways to excel. “The most exciting evolution has been mastering target marketing and creative deal structuring,” says Glass, who notched $502.1 million in sales last year. “Helping clients secure great deals and build equity despite broader economic shifts has been incredibly rewarding.” Neyshia Go Courtesy of Subject Neyshia Go SOTHEBY’S INTERNATIONAL REALTY With $1 billion in career sales, Go runs The Go Group, Sotheby’s No. 1 realty team in SoCal. Specializing in new development and investment opportunities, her team oversees the marketing for the 44-floor Park Elm Residences at Century Plaza, where they have sold $45 million worth of properties in the past nine months. “I believe the market will continue to be defined by nuances that affect each of the individual neighborhoods in Los Angeles,” she says. Jon Grauman Courtesy of Subject Jon Grauman RESIDENT GROUP In 2025, the former Buying Beverly Hills star left The Agency to form the boutique brokerage Resident Group with Lauren Grauman and Adam Rosenfeld. They’ve emerged on the scene with a bang. In April, Grauman and Rosenfeld, alongside Bennett Bidwell, repped Guess CEO Carlos Alberini and his wife, Andrea, in their sale of Bruce Willis’ former Benedict Canyon mansion for $41.25 million. Jack Harris & Michael Fahimian Courtesy of Subject (2) Jack Harris & Michael Fahimian THE BEVERLY HILLS ESTATES The super team of Harris and Fahimian had another blockbuster year, accumulating a total transaction volume of $872 million. The duo now holds the most expensive listing in the world: the $400 million, 39-bedroom Chalon Estate in Bel-Air. “Wellness is the number one priority right now,” the duo told THR . “A great gym, sauna, steam room, cold and hot plunge and a dedicated recovery area are huge bonuses.” James Harris Courtesy of Subject James Harris CAROLWOOD ESTATES Now the head of Harris & Partners inside Carolwood, Million Dollar Listing’ s Harris has said goodbye to his longtime partnership with David Parnes. In April, he sold Lizzo’s Beverly Hills estate for $11.2 million. With $275 million in deals in the past six months, he also successfully repped the seller of the $10.35 million Sherman Oaks abode purchased by Macaulay Culkin and Brenda Song. Clients include Rihanna and A$AP Rocky, Robbie Williams and James Corden. “Today’s luxury buyer,” he notes, “wants a home that’s ready to enjoy from day one.” Juliette Hohnen Courtesy of Subject Juliette Hohnen DOUGLAS ELLIMAN The Hollywood insider and former MTV VJ continues to rake in marquee sales in today’s overloaded market. With a celebrity roster that includes Rami Malek, Emilia Clarke, Maria Bello, Chris Weitz, Elijah Wood, Sonya Walger and Dan O’Shannon, Hohnen maintains a keen read on the zeitgeist. “The biggest amenity in L.A. right now is a mahjong room,” she says. “I’ve been playing for a few years, and it gives me great joy to see a room devoted to mahjong!” Marci Kays & Jonathan Mogharrabi Courtesy of Subject (2) Marci Kays & Jonathan Mogharrabi CAROLWOOD ESTATES In August 2025, Kays and Mogharrabi represented Brad Pitt in his purchase of David Keuning’s Outpost Estates enclave for $12 million and sold Pitt’s “Steel House” to Austin Butler for $5.2 million. In February, they also repped Fear of God founder Jerry Lorenzo’s sale of his Los Feliz home for $8.6 million. Says Mogharrabi, “It’s been exciting to see these neighborhoods continue to evolve and reach new levels.” Aaron Kirman Courtesy of Subject Aaron Kirman CHRISTIE’S INTERNATIONAL REAL ESTATE SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA Since Kirman launched Christie’s SoCal operation in 2022, it has scaled to more than 300 agents across multiple offices. Three years later, it hit $4.2 billion in total sales volume. Kirman scored $912 million in sales from July 2025 to July 2026, including the recent $47 million sale of the Beverly Hills brutalist estate of Oakley founder James Jannard, which is tied for the highest-priced sale in Beverly Hills this year. He also sold a Beverly Hills home once owned by Mark Wahlberg for $22 million. Craig Knizek Courtesy of Subject Craig Knizek THE AGENCY Knizek has generated more than $1.2 billion in career sales. In February, he represented Macaulay Culkin and Brenda Song in the off-market sale of their Toluca Lake estate for $14.25 million. He also represented the buyer of Lori Loughlin and Mossimo Giannulli’s $12.65 million Hidden Hills estate and sold the residence of legendary songwriters Alan and Marilyn Bergman. “As state housing laws encourage greater density, luxury is defined by personal space,” Knizek says. Weston Littlefield & Alex Howe Courtesy of Subject (2) Weston Littlefield & Alex Howe CHRISTIE’S INTERNATIONAL REAL ESTATE SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA Littlefield and Howe helped spur post-fire redevelopment in August 2025, representing a foreign investor in acquiring nine oceanfront lots on Malibu’s La Costa Beach for more than $65 million. Their clients include Restoration Hardware CEO Gary Friedman, Saw franchise producer Oren Koules and, reportedly, Kristen Wiig. “There really isn’t another market quite like Los Angeles, because every neighborhood has its own identity,” Littlefield says. Linda May Courtesy of Subject Linda May CAROLWOOD ESTATES The venerable broker remains at the top of her game. This year, she held the co-listing on Tom Cruise’s former Beverly Hills estate, which billionaire financier Leon Black sold for $47 million in March in an off-market deal. In July, she made history selling the penthouse in West Hollywood’s Sierra Towers for a record-breaking $36 million. “The market has definitely slowed compared to the frenzy we experienced a few years ago, and buyers are taking more time to make decisions,” she says. “They’re thoughtful, selective and expect value. Courtesy of the Agency Jade Mills Courtesy of Subject Jade Mills COLDWELL BANKER “Every market presents opportunities,” says Mills. “It has been especially meaningful to continue helping clients achieve exceptional results in this more selective and more difficult market.” With more than $9 billion in career sales, she continues to make big deals. In March, Mills sold the Beverly Hills mansion of former Windsor Healthcare CEO Lee Samson for $30.3 million. Michael & Myra Nourmand Courtesy of Subject (2) Michael & Myra Nourmand NOURMAND AND ASSOCIATES This year, the mother-and-son team brokered the sales of the former Malibu home of Barry Manilow and, later, Pink for $13.75 million and Tom Petty’s storied Malibu estate, which went for $11.2 million. “Not only was the property reminiscent of the Huntington Gardens,” Myra says of Petty’s place, “but it still had Tom Petty’s personality throughout, including his pre-wired studio. Last fall, he sold Bella Thorne’s Topanga Canyon home for $4 million. He now holds the co-listing of the $88 million Bel-Air contemporary megamansion developed by Michael Chen’s Luxford Group. David Parnes Courtesy of Subject David Parnes CAROLWOOD ESTATES This is Parnes’ first time on the list since splitting with partner James Harris. With $140 million in sales in the past six months, he seems to be handling the breakup well. His standout deals include the August 2025 sale of a $23 million Bird Street mansion featured in Entourage and Kevin Williamson’s Beverly Hills Post Office Estate for $21 million. “From a design perspective, we’re seeing a move away from homes that feel like museums,” he says. “Natural stone, warmer woods and homes with character are replacing the ultra-minimalist look that dominated for years.” Lea Porter Courtesy of Subject Lea Porter THE BEVERLY HILLS ESTATES In only four and a half years since returning to luxury real estate, Porter has surpassed $1 billion in sales. In April, she sold Daphna Ziman’s historic Beverly Hills Tudor-style estate once owned by Harry Warner for $27.25 million alongside co-listers Jade Mills and Joyce Rey. “A particular highlight has been representing the longtime Beverly Hills estate of Pat Boone,” she says of the past year. Kurt Rappaport Courtesy of Subject Kurt Rappaport WESTSIDE ESTATE AGENCY The elusive King of Hollywood Brokers had another banner year with more than $1 billion in sales. An agent for celebrities including David Geffen, David Ellison, Tom Brady and Beyoncé and Jay-Z, in May he held the listing for producer Joe Roth’s Beverly Hills estate, which went for $21.5 million. Joyce Rey Courtesy of Subject Joyce Rey COLDWELL BANKER The grande dame of Los Angeles real estate made her very first sale in 1974 — no less prestigious a property than the estate of Christina Onassis. More than 50 years later, the “billionaire’s broker” still loves what she does. “Every listing and client I work with excites me,” she says. Rey currently holds the co-listing (alongside Jade Mills) to Joni Mitchell’s former $26.99 million Malibu beach house.
